newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe feed trade to fill nearby needs on sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Europe feed trade to fill nearby needs on sell-off.

text.p: The European meals trade will be concentrating on filling nearby needs this week as continued volatility on soycomplex futures in Chicago makes any commitment further out too risky, market sources said on Monday.

"I would advise compounders to use this as a buying opportunity to cover nearby positions," market analyst Arie van Dijk of statisticians Stigevo said. "But only for April and May needs, the market will be coming off after that."

Heavy fund selling battered U.S. soymeal futures on Friday, pushing down the May and July soymeal positions the full $10.00 limit, where they stayed until the close. CBOT beans ended the day the 30-cent a bushel limit down at $8.41.
Traders noted rumours of China re-selling U.S. soymeal on world markets, news Brazilian beans are being shipped to the United States and a slow U.S. soybean crush were all pressuring factors.

But van Dijk said futures prices could be on the way back up by the end of the week, with beans possibly even hitting nine dollars again. A focus for the market this week will be USDA issuing supply/demand figures for soybeans on Friday, he said.
Away from the soycomplex, market sources said they expected an increase in European demand for cornglutenfeed, citruspulp and palmkernel expellers, sparked by the new milk quota season.

Cattle feeding for milk had wound down in the early part of the year as milk quotas had been exceeded but with a new season in Germany and the Netherlands starting on April 1, increased demand for these products from farmers could be expected.
This could push up Malaysian palmkernel expellers prices in particular, which at around $110 a tonne were still relatively cheap, traders said.
But the strong dollar -- which makes physical purchases for European currency holders more expensive -- would also act as an additional deterrent to trade in the near term.

But again, further out business would be limited as the appearance of the South American crop here in the summer and expectations of high U.S. soybean plantings could pressure positions from August onwards.

And an other reason for operators not to rush into the meals and feeds market is competition from feed grains, which although have risen in price slightly in the last last couple of weeks, were still relatively cheap compared to meal.
